mcqs.q: Dental anxiety and phobia most importantly result in:
mcqs.explain: Dental anxiety and phobia result in avoidance of dental care — a frequent problem and a source of stress for the dentist.

mcqs.q: Which is a SUBJECTIVE method of assessing dental anxiety?
mcqs.explain: Subjective evaluation uses self-reporting on fear and anxiety scales; BP, pulse oximetry and GSR are objective measures.

mcqs.q: Which is an OBJECTIVE measure used to assess a patient's anxiety?
mcqs.explain: Objective assessment includes blood pressure, pulse rate, pulse oximetry, finger temperature and galvanic skin response.

mcqs.q: Assessment allows patients to be categorised as:
opts: Mildly, moderately, or highly anxious, or dental phobic
mcqs.explain: Subjective and objective assessment enables categorization as mildly, moderately, or highly anxious, or dental phobic.

mcqs.q: Broadly, dental anxiety can be managed by:
mcqs.explain: Dental anxiety is managed by psychotherapeutic interventions, pharmacological interventions, or a combination of both.

mcqs.q: Pharmacological management of the anxious patient uses:
mcqs.explain: Pharmacologically, anxious patients can be managed using either sedation or general anesthesia.

mcqs.q: Which should be the PRIMARY focus of the dental team for anxious patients?
opts: Psychological therapies (efficient long-term, enabling future care)
mcqs.explain: Psychological therapies are efficient long-term with positive effects, enabling patients to seek future care — the primary focus of the dental team.

mcqs.q: According to Tickle et al. (2012), actual pain during procedures affects approximately:
mcqs.explain: Occurrence of pain during procedures may be low — affecting less than 25% of general dental practice patients.

mcqs.q: Despite low actual pain, dental care-related anxiety persists largely because of:
opts: Public perception that dental care is highly associated with pain
mcqs.explain: Public perceptions are that dental care is highly associated with pain, so anxiety/fear stay closely related to oral pain.

mcqs.q: The emotional reaction to pain is used by the patient as a:
opts: Cue to escape or avoid the situation
mcqs.explain: The unpleasantness of pain and its implications drive an emotional reaction used as a cue to escape and/or avoid the situation.

mcqs.q: Which is a BIOLOGICAL factor affecting pain perception?
mcqs.explain: Biological factors include innervation and genetics; emotional, cognitive and environmental factors are separate categories.

mcqs.q: Provider communication and the stimuli of the operatory are which type of pain factor?
mcqs.explain: Environmental determinants include the stimulus characteristics of the dental operatory and provider communication.

mcqs.q: Anxiety, fear, stress and depression are which type of pain factor?
mcqs.explain: Emotional determinants include anxiety, fear, stress and depression.

mcqs.q: Catastrophizing and memory are which type of pain factor?
mcqs.explain: Cognitive components include catastrophizing and memory.

mcqs.q: ‘Catastrophizing’ means:
opts: Imagining the worst possible outcome of an action or event
mcqs.explain: Catastrophizing means to imagine the worst possible outcome of an action or event.

mcqs.q: The dentist–patient relationship significantly affects pain because its key component is:
mcqs.explain: An important component of the provider–patient relationship is communication, which affects the experience and expression of pain.

mcqs.q: Patients with POORER relationships with their provider are:
opts: Less likely to discuss pain and at greater risk of not receiving appropriate care
mcqs.explain: Patients with poorer-quality relationships were less likely to discuss a pain problem and at greater risk of not receiving appropriate dental care.

mcqs.q: Patients report LESS pain when the provider communicates:
opts: Confidence in the intervention (vs being unsure or hesitant)
mcqs.explain: When providers communicated confidence in an intervention, patients reported less pain than when the provider was unsure or hesitant.

mcqs.q: Besides confidence, which provider behaviour reduces pain responding?
mcqs.explain: Two facets of communication affecting pain are provider confidence and provider behaviour described as ‘warm and friendly’.

mcqs.q: ‘Distraction’ as a pain-control technique means:
opts: Shifting the patient's attention to a more pleasant stimulus
mcqs.explain: Distraction shifts the patient's attention away from the painful situation to another, more pleasant stimulus.

mcqs.q: Which was found MORE effective at reducing discomfort?
opts: Watching TV or playing a video game
mcqs.explain: Watching a television program or playing a video game was more effective at reducing patient discomfort than listening to an audiotape.

mcqs.q: Regarding ‘predictability’, providing information about the procedure generally:
opts: Increases predictability and decreases pain & anxiety (though some prefer less info)
mcqs.explain: More information generally increases predictability and decreases pain/anxiety, although some individuals prefer less information to cope.

mcqs.q: Effective ways to decrease the pain experience via EMOTIONAL determinants include:
opts: Reducing anxiety/fear, improving mood, and focusing attention away from pain
Highlighting how painful it will be
mcqs.explain: Reducing anxiety and fear, improving mood, and focusing attention away from pain can effectively decrease the pain experience.

mcqs.q: Patients with HIGH dental anxiety tend to have:
opts: Greater expectations and recall of pain
mcqs.explain: Dental patients with high anxiety tend to have greater expectations and recall of pain.

mcqs.q: Moderate (conscious) sedation during oral surgery is associated with:
opts: Memory of less pain and anxiety one month later
mcqs.explain: Moderate (conscious) sedation has the desired effect of being associated with memory of less pain and anxiety one month after the procedure.

mcqs.q: Patients with higher levels of dental anxiety and fear tend to:
opts: Have more pain sensitivity (less tolerance) and more irregular attendance
mcqs.explain: Higher anxiety/fear is linked to more pain sensitivity (less tolerance), more reported pain, and a greater likelihood of irregular attendance.

mcqs.q: Variants of the MC1R gene (associated with red hair) are linked to:
opts: More dental anxiety, fear of pain, and greater pain sensitivity
mcqs.explain: Individuals with MC1R gene variants (red hair) seem to have more dental anxiety, fear of dental pain, and greater pain sensitivity.

mcqs.q: Regarding gender, the source notes that USUALLY:
opts: Women report more fear of dental pain than men
Men report more fear than women
mcqs.explain: Women usually report more fear of dental pain, while males reported less such fear.

mcqs.q: Patients of LOWER socioeconomic status (SES) tend to:
opts: Report greater orofacial pain and greater behavioral impact
mcqs.explain: Patients of lower SES report greater orofacial pain and have greater behavioral impact from the pain compared with high-SES patients.

mcqs.q: Regarding age, who is MORE likely to report pain?
opts: Younger individuals (older adults of high SES report less)
mcqs.explain: Younger individuals are more likely to report pain, while older adults of high SES are less likely to report pain.

saqs.q: How is dental anxiety assessed (give subjective and objective methods)?
saqs.a: Subjective: self-reporting on fear & anxiety scales. Objective: blood pressure, pulse rate, pulse oximetry, finger temperature, galvanic skin response. Together they categorise patients as mildly/moderately/highly anxious or dental phobic.

saqs.q: How can dental anxiety be managed?
saqs.a: By psychotherapeutic, pharmacological (sedation or general anesthesia), or both, depending on anxiety level/patient/situation. Psychological therapies are efficient long-term and enable future care — the primary focus.

saqs.q: List the categories of factors that affect the perception of pain.
saqs.a: Biological (innervation, genetics), Environmental (operatory stimuli, communication), Emotional (anxiety, fear, stress, depression), Cognitive (catastrophizing, memory), and patient characteristics (age, gender, race, culture, SES).

saqs.q: How do the dentist–patient relationship and communication affect pain?
saqs.a: The relationship strongly affects the experience/expression of pain; its key component is communication. Poorer relationships → less likely to discuss pain → greater risk. Provider confidence and a warm, friendly manner lead patients to report less pain.

saqs.q: Explain ‘distraction’ and ‘predictability’ as ways to reduce pain.
saqs.a: Distraction = shifting attention to a more pleasant stimulus (music, TV, video game, VR) — TV/games beat audiotapes. Predictability = giving information about the procedural & sensory experience increases predictability and decreases pain/anxiety (though some prefer less information).

saqs.q: How do patient characteristics (genetics, age, gender, SES) affect dental pain?
saqs.a: Genetics: MC1R (red hair) variants → more anxiety & pain sensitivity. Age: younger report more pain; older high-SES report less. Gender: women usually report more fear of dental pain. SES: lower SES → greater orofacial pain & behavioral impact.
